title: Game of Thrones Takes the Stage With Ambitious RSC Prequel The Mad King
excerpt: The Royal Shakespeare Company's four-hour epic brings young Ned Stark, Robert Baratheon, and the Tourney at Harrenhal to life, with previews already drawing sold-out crowds and mixed early reactions.
body:
• Game of Thrones: The Mad King, a four-hour stage prequel, began previews on July 20 at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon, with the official opening night set for August 8.
  • Michael Abubakar leads a 32-member cast as young Ned Stark, alongside Callum Woodhouse as Robert Baratheon and Michael Shaeffer as King Aerys II Targaryen.
  • The entire run through September 5 is sold out, though early preview cancellations due to "unforeseen delays" angered some ticket holders.
  • Early audience reactions are split — one preview drew a standing ovation while a New York Post reviewer called it "like binge-watching HBO onstage."

The world of Westeros has found a new home — not on HBO, but on the boards of the Royal Shakespeare Theatre. Game of Thrones: The Mad King, a sweeping four-hour stage prequel executive produced by George R.R. Martin, began preview performances in Stratford-upon-Avon on July 20 and is already sold out through its September 5 closing date.

Written by Duncan Macmillan (Lungs, Every Brilliant Thing) and directed by Dominic Cooke, the production is set roughly 15 years before the events of Martin's novels, centering on the legendary Tourney at Harrenhal — the jousting competition that would ultimately ignite Robert's Rebellion and reshape the Seven Kingdoms.

A New Generation of Westerosi Faces

The RSC unveiled the full 32-member cast in late May, with Michael Abubakar stepping into Sean Bean's iconic role as a younger Ned Stark. Callum Woodhouse plays Lord Robert Baratheon, while Michael Shaeffer takes on the title role of the paranoid and volatile King Aerys II Targaryen. Noah Ritter portrays Prince Rhaegar Targaryen, and Harmony Rose-Bremner plays Lyanna Stark — the pair whose ill-fated romance at the tournament would trigger a war.

The ensemble also includes Maxim Ays as Jaime Lannister, Daisy Franks as Cersei Lannister, Elizabeth Ayodele as Elia Martell, Marcello Walton as Lord Tywin Lannister, Edem-Ita Duke as Oberyn Martell, and Marty Breen as Catelyn Stark. Brandon Stark, Ned's older brother who was never shown in the HBO series, also finally makes an appearance.

"I love this cast — they bring all the strengths, flaws and intricacies within these characters that drive this important chapter of Westerosi history. They have a fire in them, and I can't wait to see them bring that fire to the stage."

— George R.R. Martin, Creator and Executive Producer

Sold Out, But Not Without Turbulence

The production's commercial success is undeniable — every performance through its run is sold out. But the first week of previews hit turbulence when the RSC cancelled at least one Saturday performance, citing "unforeseen delays" related to the production's ambitious scope. Ticket holders, some of whom had booked hotels in Stratford specifically for the show, vented their frustration on social media and Reddit.

The RSC offered full refunds but acknowledged that rebooking options were limited given the sold-out run. "Owing to the ambitious and epic nature of this production and faced with a number of unforeseen delays, we require additional time to bring Game of Thrones: The Mad King to a public audience," the company said in a statement, according to Deadline.

Early Reactions: Standing Ovation Meets Skepticism

The first preview reportedly received a standing ovation, according to Nerdist. But not everyone was swept up in the spectacle. A reviewer for the New York Post who caught a preview described the experience as "like binge-watching HBO onstage," praising Michael Shaeffer's compelling performance as Aerys and the stunning costumes and dragon puppets, but questioning the production's theatrical ambition.

"There's literally no reason for it to be a play. It plays like a spec script for an HBO prequel and spends too much time treading water in favor of exposition."

— New York Post preview reviewer

The RSC, however, has a track record of transforming sprawling literary properties into theatrical triumphs — from Nicholas Nickleby to the early staging of Les Misérables, a show many critics initially underestimated.

A Franchise That Keeps Expanding

The stage production arrives in a banner year for the Game of Thrones franchise. A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms debuted its first season to a 94% Rotten Tomatoes score, and House of the Dragon Season 3 premiered on June 21. The Mad King marks the franchise's first foray into live theatre, and its success could open the door to West End or Broadway transfers.

For the millions of Game of Thrones fans across India — where the series routinely trended as one of the most-watched international shows — the RSC production adds another reason to plan a UK trip this summer. The official opening night is set for August 8, when full critical reviews are expected to drop.

What's Next

All eyes turn to that opening night. If The Mad King can tighten its four-hour runtime and harness its theatrical elements as effectively as its spectacle, it could follow in the footsteps of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child as a franchise stage phenomenon. Whether Martin's Westeros belongs on stage as much as on screen is a question audiences in Stratford are already answering — with their wallets, at least.
nri_angle: Game of Thrones commands a massive fanbase across India, and the RSC production's sold-out run and potential transfer could draw Indian theatre enthusiasts and cultural tourists to Stratford-upon-Avon.
